title: Askia Muhammad Takes Songhai
text: A general named Muhammad Ture seized the throne of the Songhai Empire, the biggest state West Africa had ever seen. As Askia Muhammad he backed Islamic scholars in Timbuktu and made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca. His tomb in Gao, a mud-brick pyramid bristling with wooden beams, still stands today.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Muhammad I Askia)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Tomb of Askia)

title: A Teenage Shah Crowned in Tabriz
text: Ismail, only about 14 years old, was crowned shah in Tabriz and founded the Safavid dynasty. He declared Twelver Shia Islam the official faith of his realm, a choice that still shapes Iran's identity today. He was also a poet, writing verses in Azerbaijani Turkish under the pen name Khatai.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Esmail I Safawi: i. Biography; ii. His Poetry)

title: Portugal Storms Rich Kilwa
text: Kilwa was a wealthy Swahili trading city that minted its own copper coins and built a grand coral-stone mosque. In 1505 a Portuguese fleet under Francisco de Almeida seized the city and built a fort there, as Portugal tried to control the rich Indian Ocean trade routes. The island's ruins are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Ruins of Songo Mnara)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Francisco de Almeida; Kilwa)

title: The Poet King of Vijayanagara
text: Krishnadevaraya took the throne of the Vijayanagara Empire. A Portuguese visitor thought its capital at Hampi looked as large as Rome and called it the best-provided city in the world. The king was also a writer: he composed a long Telugu poem, and tradition says his court was graced by eight master poets, nicknamed the 'elephants of the eight directions'.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (India: The Vijayanagar empire)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Group of Monuments at Hampi)

title: Michelangelo Finishes the Ceiling
text: After four years of work, Michelangelo unveiled his paintings across the Sistine Chapel ceiling, including the famous Creation of Adam. Despite the legend, he painted standing on a scaffold he designed, not lying on his back. He even wrote a grumpy poem to a friend about the aches it caused.

source.name: Vatican Museums (Sistine Chapel: The Ceiling)

source2.name: Casa Buonarroti (via Google Arts & Culture), sonnet and self-portrait sheet, AB XIII 111

title: An Admiral's Map on Gazelle Skin
text: The Ottoman admiral Piri Reis drew a world map on gazelle-skin parchment, combining around twenty older sources, including one he said came from Columbus. It shows the coasts of Africa and South America. Only a piece survives, and it lay forgotten until it was found in Istanbul's Topkapı Palace in 1929.

source.name: Ohio State University, 'Wind Rose' map history site (1513 / World Map / Piri Reis)

title: Luther's 95 Theses
text: A monk and professor named Martin Luther wrote 95 arguments against the Church selling 'indulgences', payments said to shorten punishment after death. Thanks to the new printing presses, copies spread across Germany within weeks. His protest grew into the Protestant Reformation, splitting Western Christianity for good.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Ninety-five Theses)

title: Lapulapu Defeats Magellan
text: Ferdinand Magellan demanded that Lapulapu, a chief on Mactan Island, obey the king of Spain. Lapulapu refused, and when Magellan's men waded ashore through the shallows, his warriors overwhelmed them and killed Magellan. Today the Philippines honors Lapulapu: a city on Mactan and a state award, the Order of Lapu-Lapu, bear his name.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Ferdinand Magellan: Discovery of the Strait)

source2.name: VERA Files (fact check on Lapulapu, citing NHCP)

title: Babur Founds the Mughal Empire
text: Babur, a prince from Central Asia, beat the much larger army of the Delhi Sultan at Panipat, helped by cannons and matchlock guns. The victory began the Mughal Empire. Babur wrote a frank memoir, the Baburnama, where he grumbled that India lacked the good melons and grapes of his homeland.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Babur)

source2.name: Project Gutenberg: The Babur-nama in English, tr. A. S. Beveridge (1922)

title: Atahualpa's Room of Ransom
text: Francisco Pizarro's small Spanish force ambushed and captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca. To win his freedom, Atahualpa offered to fill a room with gold, and his people brought gold and silver from all over the empire. The Spanish executed him anyway in 1533, opening the way to conquering the Inca Empire.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Atahuallpa)

title: The Americas' First Printing Press
text: Giovanni Paoli, an Italian printer known in Spanish as Juan Pablos, sailed from Seville and set up the first printing press in the Americas in Mexico City. The first known book from it was a short Christian guide written in both Spanish and Nahuatl, the Aztec language. Sadly, no copy of that book has survived.

source.name: Library of Congress blog (Hispanic Heritage Month: Early Titles by the Americas' First Printing Press)

title: Sher Shah's Silver Rupiya
text: Sher Shah Suri drove the Mughal emperor Humayun out of India and ruled North India for five busy years. He issued a standard silver coin called the rupiya, the ancestor of today's rupee. He also improved the great road across North India, with rest houses for travelers along the way.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Sher Shah of Sur)

source2.name: Reserve Bank of India, Currency Museum: Mughal coinage

title: Guns Wash Up in Japan
text: In 1543 a ship carrying Portuguese traders sought shelter from a storm on the small island of Tanegashima. The local lord bought two of their matchlock guns and had a local swordsmith copy them. Soon Japanese workshops were making guns by the thousands, the weapon was simply called a 'tanegashima', and samurai warfare changed forever.

source.name: EBSCO Research Starters (M. McCaskey, 'Europeans Begin Trade with Japan', 2022)

source2.name: Japan Tourism Agency multilingual commentary database (MLIT), 'Guns in Early Modern Japan'

title: Tomatoes Enter a European Book
text: Italian doctor Pietro Andrea Mattioli published a book of plants with the earliest known European mention of the tomato, a newcomer from the Americas. He called it a new kind of eggplant that turned red or gold and was cooked like one. Ten years later he named it pomi d'oro, 'golden apples'.

source.name: PeerJ (van Andel et al., 'Sixteenth-century tomatoes in Europe', 2022), PubMed Central

title: Spain Debates Conquest Itself
text: In 1550 Spain's king halted new conquests in the Americas and called a formal debate on how Indigenous Americans should be treated. Friar Bartolomé de las Casas argued against their conquest; scholar Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda argued it was justified. The judges were slow to rule and conquest went on, but the debate was a watershed in thinking about human rights.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Bartolome de Las Casas)

source2.name: History Today (Mathew Lyons, 'The Valladolid Debate on the Rights of Indigenous People', vol. 73 no. 8, 2023)

title: The Deadliest Earthquake Ever
text: On January 23, 1556, a huge earthquake struck Shaanxi province in central China. About 830,000 people are thought to have died, the highest toll of any recorded earthquake. Many lived in yaodong, cozy cave homes carved into soft loess hills, which collapsed when the ground shook.

source.name: USGS (Cool Earthquake Facts)

source2.name: USGS (Today in Earthquake History, January 23)

title: St. Augustine Is Founded
text: Spanish admiral Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded St. Augustine on land of the Timucua people. It is the oldest continuously inhabited city founded by Europeans in the mainland United States, older than Jamestown by 42 years. Its stone fort, the Castillo de San Marcos, was built from shell-filled coquina rock.

source.name: National Park Service (St. Augustine Town Plan Historic District)

source2.name: National Park Service (The First Thanksgiving; Castillo de San Marcos)

title: Ming China Reopens the Sea
text: The Ming dynasty had long banned private sea trade. In 1567 the new Longqing emperor opened the port of Yuegang in Fujian, licensing Chinese merchants to trade abroad, though Japanese merchants were still shut out. Nearby kilns boomed, and porcelain from Yuegang's trade flowed to Spanish merchants in Manila, who shipped it across the Pacific on the galleons.

source.name: J. K. Kung & C. Ma, 'Autarky and the Rise and Fall of Piracy in Ming China' (working paper, later J. Economic History)

source2.name: Guanyu Wang (Art Museum, CUHK), 'Chinese Porcelain in the Manila Galleon Trade', in Archaeology of Manila Galleon Seaports (Springer, 2019)

title: Akbar's Red Sandstone City
text: Mughal emperor Akbar began building a brand-new capital of red sandstone at Fatehpur Sikri. In its House of Worship he hosted debates where Muslim scholars were joined by Hindu pandits, Parsi priests, Jain monks and Jesuits. The court left after about 15 years, possibly over water shortages, and the city survives in good condition.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Fatehpur Sikri; Akbar)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Fatehpur Sikri)

title: Li Shizhen's Giant Medicine Book
text: Doctor Li Shizhen finished the Compendium of Materia Medica after decades of travel, reading and research. It describes nearly 1,900 medicines from plants, animals and minerals, with some 11,000 prescriptions. He tried remedies on patients and even on himself to test what earlier doctors and scholars had claimed.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Li Shizhen)

source2.name: Harvard Magazine (Carla Nappi, 'Li Shizhen', Jan.-Feb. 2010)

title: Betrayal at Honnō-ji Temple
text: Oda Nobunaga was close to uniting war-torn Japan when his own general, Akechi Mitsuhide, attacked him at Honnō-ji temple in Kyoto. Nobunaga died as the temple burned. Yasuke, an African man who served Nobunaga as a retainer, was in Kyoto that night and fought in the clash.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Yasuke, by Thomas Lockley)

title: The Lost Colony of Roanoke
text: About 118 English men, women and children sailed to Roanoke Island in 1587, and a baby named Virginia Dare became the first English child born in the Americas. When John White finally returned with supplies in 1590, the settlers had vanished. The only clue was the word 'CROATOAN' carved into a post, the name of a nearby Native people and their island.

source.name: National Park Service, Fort Raleigh NHS (1587: The Lost Colony)

source2.name: National Park Service (North Carolina: Fort Raleigh National Historic Site)

title: Morocco's Guns Topple Songhai
text: Morocco's sultan Ahmad al-Mansur sent an army of mercenaries under Pasha Judar, many armed with muskets, against the Songhai Empire of West Africa. At Tondibi in March 1591 they routed a far larger Songhai army of archers and cavalry, reportedly some 27,000 strong. The once-mighty Songhai Empire never recovered.

source.name: Journal of African History (L. Kaba, 'Archers, Musketeers, and Mosquitoes: The Moroccan Invasion of the Sudan and the Songhay Resistance 1591-1612'), Cambridge

title: Fort Jesus Guards Mombasa
text: The Portuguese began building Fort Jesus to control Mombasa's harbor on the Swahili coast. Its Italian architect, Giovanni Battista Cairati, based its layout on the Renaissance ideal of the human body's proportions. It changed hands many times, and Omani Arabs captured it in 1698 after a siege of nearly three years.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Fort Jesus, Mombasa), text via UNESCO open data API

source2.name: National Museums of Kenya (Fort Jesus)

title: The Battle That Made the Shoguns
text: Tens of thousands of samurai clashed in a foggy mountain valley at Sekigahara. Tokugawa Ieyasu won after several enemy commanders switched sides mid-battle. Three years later he became shogun, and his family ruled a mostly peaceful Japan for more than 250 years.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Battle of Sekigahara, by Myles Hudson)

title: Matteo Ricci's Map of the World
text: Italian Jesuit Matteo Ricci, who learned Chinese and wore local dress, made a giant world map with his collaborator Li Zhizao. It was the first map in Chinese to show the Americas. Unlike European maps, which put the Atlantic in the middle, it placed China and the Pacific Ocean near the center, in keeping with Chinese mapmaking traditions.

source.name: University of Minnesota Libraries, James Ford Bell Library (1602 World Map of Matteo Ricci)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Matteo Ricci, by Joseph Hsing-san Shih)

title: First Europeans Land in Australia
text: Dutch captain Willem Janszoon sailed the little ship Duyfken to Cape York Peninsula, making the first recorded European landing in Australia. He thought it was part of New Guinea. Meetings with Aboriginal people went badly, and the land had been their home for at least 50,000 years already.

source.name: Western Australian Museum (Dirk Hartog: Pre-1616)

source2.name: Australian National Maritime Museum (1606: Contact at Cape Keerweer)

title: Heo Jun's Mirror of Medicine
text: Royal doctor Heo Jun finished the Dongui Bogam, a 25-volume encyclopedia of East Asian medicine. He worked on it for years, even while in exile, and stressed preventing illness through healthy living. It is still used in Korean medicine and is listed in UNESCO's Memory of the World.

source.name: J Community Hosp Intern Med Perspect (2021), 'Heo Jun: physician of the people' (PMC7850328)

source2.name: Korea.net (official website of the Republic of Korea), 'What is the Dongui Bogam?'

title: Nurhaci Founds the Later Jin
text: Jurchen chief Nurhaci declared himself khan of a new state, the Later Jin. He organized his people into the 'Eight Banners', military-social units marked by colored flags, and had a writing system made for his language. His heirs renamed the people Manchus and went on to conquer all of China as the Qing dynasty.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Nurhachi, by Franz H. Michael)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Banner system)

title: Manhattan Changes Hands
text: Dutch director Peter Minuit traded goods valued at 60 guilders with the Lenape for Manhattan Island, where the town of New Amsterdam was growing. The Lenape probably saw it as sharing the land, not selling it forever. The busy fur-trading town later became New York City.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Peter Minuit)

title: The Last Aurochs Dies
text: Aurochs were giant wild cattle, ancestors of today's cows, that once roamed across Eurasia and North Africa. The last ones survived in Poland, where kings kept the sole right to hunt them and protected them in the royal forests of Jaktorów. The very last one, a cow, died a natural death in 1627, as a royal inspection reported in 1630.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (aurochs)

source2.name: Animal Genetic Resources (Cambridge), 'History of the aurochs in Poland'

title: A Samurai in Siam's Court
text: Yamada Nagamasa, a Japanese adventurer, led the Japanese quarter of Ayutthaya, home to perhaps 500 to 1,000 people. He helped revive trade with Japan, commanded the Japanese guard at the Siamese king's palace and was ennobled. Caught up in a royal power struggle, he was sent south as governor of Ligor (Nakhon Si Thammarat) and poisoned there in 1630.

source.name: The Historical Journal (Cambridge): 'Narrating Japan's Early Modern Southern Expansion'

source2.name: Journal of the Siam Society 95 (2007), Iwamoto, 'Yamada Nagamasa and His Relations with Siam'

title: Ethiopia's City of Castles
text: Emperor Fasilides made Gondar his permanent capital after Ethiopian rulers had moved their royal camps around for centuries. He built a stone castle with huge towers and battlements, plus a bathing pavilion in a pool, and later emperors added more palaces and churches. The royal enclosure, Fasil Ghebbi, mixes Ethiopian traditions with Indian, Arab and European influences.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Fasil Ghebbi, Gondar Region), text via UNESCO open data API

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Gonder)

title: A Handbook of How Things Are Made
text: Scholar Song Yingxing, who had failed the imperial exams six times, published the Tiangong Kaiwu in 1637, a guide to Chinese technology with 123 illustrations. It explains how everyday things were made, from silk, paper and ink to wine, boats, carts and even firearms. Early in the 20th century, scholars rediscovered the book in Japan.

source.name: University of Chicago Press (Dagmar Schäfer, The Crafting of the 10,000 Things: Knowledge and Technology in Seventeenth-Century China)

source2.name: Jesus College, Cambridge: China Centre lecture by Prof. Dagmar Schäfer (Max Planck Institute for the History of Science)

title: Aceh's Century of Queens
text: Taj ul-Alam became sultana of Aceh, a powerful trading kingdom on Sumatra, after her husband died. She ruled for 34 years and was the first of four women who led Aceh one after another until 1699. Islamic literature and scholarship flourished under their rule.

source.name: Mehmet Ozay, 'Women as Rulers Phenomenon in Southeast Asian Islamic Society: The Queens of Aceh', World Journal of Islamic History and Civilization 1(3) 2011 (Universiti Teknologi Malaysia)

title: Tasman Meets Māori in Golden Bay
text: Dutch explorer Abel Tasman became the first known European to reach New Zealand. In Golden Bay, Māori in canoes attacked a small Dutch boat and four sailors were killed. Local descendants call it a cultural misunderstanding, while one archaeologist thinks the iwi was guarding its kūmara gardens. Tasman quickly sailed on north.

source.name: Princeton University Library, Pacific Islands maps exhibit: Abel Tasman

source2.name: RNZ (Radio New Zealand)

title: The Last Ming Emperor Falls
text: As rebel leader Li Zicheng's army broke into Beijing, the Chongzhen Emperor took his own life on a hill behind the Forbidden City. Weeks later a Ming general opened the Great Wall's Shanhai Pass to the Manchus. They took Beijing, and the Qing dynasty ruled China until 1912.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Chongzhen'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Wu Sangui'

title: Sailing Past Asia's Tip
text: Russian Cossack Semyon Dezhnev and his crew sailed single-deck boats called kochi around the far eastern tip of Asia, through the strait between Asia and America. They did it about 80 years before Vitus Bering, whose name the strait now carries. Dezhnev's reports lay unheeded in the archives of Yakutsk for almost a century.

source.name: Encyclopedia Arctica (Stefansson), Dartmouth College Library: 'Semen Dezhnev'

source2.name: U.S. National Park Service, Beringia: Origin

title: A Vegetable Garden Becomes Cape Town
text: Jan van Riebeeck landed for the Dutch East India Company to set up a supply station where ships could get fresh water, meat and vegetables on the long trip to Asia. The Company's Garden he started still exists. The settlement grew into Cape Town, and pushed the Khoekhoe people off their grazing lands.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Jan van Riebeeck'

source2.name: City of Cape Town, The Company's Garden

title: The Great Fire of Edo
text: Fanned by strong winds, a fire raged through Edo, Japan's crowded wooden capital, for three days. It burned about 60 percent of the city and killed somewhere between 30,000 and 100,000 people; the main tower of Edo Castle burned and was never rebuilt. Afterward the city added wide roads and embankments as firebreaks.

source.name: Tokyo Metropolitan Library, Edo-Tokyo digital museum: 'Reconstruction of the city after Great Fire of Meireki'

source2.name: Tokyo Metropolitan Library, Edo-Tokyo digital museum: Edo Castle keep

title: Koxinga Takes Taiwan
text: Koxinga, a Ming loyalist commander, besieged the Dutch Fort Zeelandia for about nine months. The Dutch surrendered and left Taiwan in early 1662. Koxinga, whose mother was Japanese, died months later, but his family ruled Taiwan until the Qing took it in 1683.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Zheng Chenggong' (Ralph C. Croizier)

title: London Burns from a Bakery
text: A fire started in a bakery on Pudding Lane and spread through London's wooden houses for four days. It destroyed over 13,000 homes and old St Paul's Cathedral. Diarist Samuel Pepys famously buried his wine and Parmesan cheese in his garden to save them.

source.name: London Museum: The Great Fire of London

source2.name: Diary of Samuel Pepys, 4 Sept 1666 (Project Gutenberg text of the primary source)

title: Shivaji Crowned at Raigad
text: Shivaji, a Maratha leader famed for lightning raids and hill forts, was crowned Chhatrapati, or emperor, at his clifftop fortress of Raigad. He had challenged the mighty Mughals and built a navy to guard the coast. The Maratha state he founded became a major power in India.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Shivaji'

source2.name: Incredible India (Ministry of Tourism, Government of India), Shivrajyabhishek Sohala

title: Tiny Animals in a Drop of Water
text: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was a Delft cloth merchant with no university education who learned to grind lenses and built tiny but powerful microscopes. Looking at water, he saw swarms of living 'animalcules', what we now call microbes, and wrote to London's Royal Society about them. Its scientists were doubtful at first, but they confirmed what he saw.

source.name: Lane N. 'The unseen world: reflections on Leeuwenhoek (1677) Concerning little animals', Phil Trans R Soc B 2015 (PMC)

source2.name: UC Museum of Paleontology, Berkeley: Antony van Leeuwenhoek

title: The Great Cavalry Charge at Vienna
text: An Ottoman army had besieged Vienna for two months when a relief force arrived. Polish King Jan III Sobieski led a massive charge of some 20,000 horsemen, spearheaded by his famous hussars, which lasted about half an hour. The siege broke, and the Ottomans slowly began losing territory in Europe.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Siege of Vienna (1683)'

source2.name: Polish History Museum (polishhistory.pl), 'The Battle of Vienna (1683): The Clash that Saved Europe'

title: China and Russia Draw a Border
text: After clashes along the Amur River, Kangxi's Qing China and Russia signed the Treaty of Nerchinsk. It was China's first treaty with a European state. The two sides had no shared language, so two Jesuit priests helped negotiate in Latin, and the final treaty was written out in Latin, Mongolian, Manchu, Chinese and Russian.

source.name: The China Project, James Carter (Saint Joseph's University), 'The near miracle that was China's first modern treaty with a European state'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Treaty of Nerchinsk'

title: Sor Juana Defends Women's Learning
text: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, a nun and the foremost poet of colonial Mexico, was told by the bishop of Puebla, writing as 'Sister Filotea', to focus on religious rather than secular studies. In 1691 she replied with a brilliant letter defending women's right to knowledge. Largely self-taught, she mastered Latin and cut her hair to punish herself for mistakes.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz'

source2.name: National Museum of Women in the Arts, 'The Tenth Muse'

title: The Fall of Free Palmares
text: For most of a century, people who escaped slavery built Palmares, a free settlement of thousands in the hills of northeast Brazil. In 1694 a colonial army destroyed its capital after a long siege. Its leader Zumbi was killed on November 20, 1695, a date Brazil now marks as Black Consciousness Day.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Palmares'

source2.name: Agência Brasil (EBC), 'Zumbi dos Palmares: a 17th century Negro leader's death is celebrated' (2003)

title: A Tsar Works in a Shipyard
text: Young Tsar Peter of Russia toured Western Europe with a huge delegation, the Grand Embassy. In Dutch shipyards he worked with his own hands as a ship's carpenter, travelling under a fake name. He brought home shipbuilders and ideas to modernize Russia.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Peter I: The Grand Embassy (1697-98)' (L. A. Nikiforov)

title: The Golden Stool of the Asante
text: According to Asante tradition, the priest Okomfo Anokye called a golden stool down from the sky onto the lap of King Osei Tutu. It is believed to house the soul of the Asante nation. The stool must never touch the ground, and even the king does not sit on it: it rests on its own chair.

source.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline: 'Gold in Asante Courtly Arts'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Golden Stool' (topic page)

title: A Capital Built on a Swamp
text: Peter the Great founded Saint Petersburg on marshy land at the mouth of the Neva River, wanting a 'window to Europe'. Tens of thousands of forced laborers drained the swamps, and many died. In 1712 it became Russia's capital, with canals and palaces designed in a European style.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'St. Petersburg: History'

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Historic Centre of Saint Petersburg (text via data.unesco.org API)

title: Mount Fuji's Last Eruption
text: Just weeks after a huge earthquake, Mount Fuji erupted from a new crater on its side. Ash fell on Edo, some 60 miles away, and the sky grew so dark that people lit candles in the daytime. Homes and fields in villages near the mountain were buried, and Fuji has not erupted since.

source.name: Koyama et al., 'Reconstruction of the 1707 Hoei eruption of Fuji Volcano', JpGU 2002 abstract (Shizuoka Univ.)

source2.name: Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program, Fujisan

title: New Orleans Is Founded
text: French colonist Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville founded a town on a sharp bend of the Mississippi River and named it after the Duke of Orléans. Built on swampy ground prone to floods, it grew into a city blending many heritages, where citizens of African descent helped make New Orleans the birthplace of jazz.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'History of New Orleans' (Joy Juanita Jackson)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'New Orleans'

title: Japan Opens to Dutch Learning
text: Shogun Tokugawa Yoshimune relaxed the ban on foreign books, as long as they weren't about Christianity. Japanese scholars began studying Dutch books on medicine, astronomy and geography, a movement called Rangaku, 'Dutch learning'. Later a group of doctors watched a dissection, were amazed by how accurate a Dutch anatomy book was, and translated it.

source.name: National Diet Library (Japan), 'Japan-Netherlands Exchange: Boom in Dutch Studies'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'rangaku'

title: Easter Day at Rapa Nui
text: Dutch explorer Jacob Roggeveen reached a remote Pacific island on Easter Sunday, so he named it Easter Island. Its people, the Rapa Nui, had carved hundreds of giant stone statues called moai. The one-day visit turned violent when the Dutch crew killed several islanders in a misunderstanding.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Easter Island' (incl. History section)

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Rapa Nui National Park (text via data.unesco.org API)

title: The Ottoman Printing Press
text: İbrahim Müteferrika, a Hungarian-born convert to Islam, became the first Muslim to run a printing press in the Ottoman Empire. Its first book, in 1729, was a big two-volume Arabic dictionary. He went on to print maps, histories and science books, but his permission covered only non-religious works, so religious texts stayed handwritten.

source.name: Library of Congress, In Custodia Legis: 'Ibrahim Muteferrika, First Muslim Printer of the Ottoman Empire' (2023)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ibrahim Muteferrika'

title: Linnaeus Names Nature
text: Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus published Systema Naturae in Leiden, a plan to sort every plant, animal and mineral into groups. The first edition was only 11 large pages, but he kept expanding it, and by the 10th edition of 1758 it was a substantial two-volume set. His two-part naming system, like Homo sapiens, is still how scientists name species.

source.name: Linnean Society of London, 'Naming Nature'

source2.name: Library of Congress catalog: Systema naturae, 1735, facsimile of the 1st ed.

title: Nader Shah Takes the Peacock Throne
text: Persian ruler Nader Shah crushed the Mughal army at Karnal and marched into Delhi. After a deadly massacre, he carried away enormous treasure, including the jeweled Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond. His empire soon stretched from the Indus River to the Caucasus Mountains.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Nāder Shah' (Ernest Tucker)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Nādir Shāh'

title: A Pact in the Desert Oasis
text: In the mud-brick oasis town of Diriyah, local ruler Muhammad ibn Saud made an alliance with preacher Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab. The ruler would back the preacher's strict reform movement, and the preacher would support the ruler. Their pact founded the first Saudi state, ancestor of today's Saudi Arabia.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: At-Turaif District in ad-Dir'iyah

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab

title: An Encyclopedia of Everything
text: Denis Diderot and Jean le Rond d'Alembert published the first volume of the Encyclopédie, aiming to gather all human knowledge. It covered crafts and machines as well as philosophy, with detailed illustrated plates. Its questioning ideas angered authorities, who banned it, but it kept being printed and became a symbol of the Enlightenment.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Encyclopédie

title: Lisbon's Triple Disaster
text: On All Saints' Day morning, a massive earthquake shook Lisbon while churches were full. A tsunami followed, then fires burned for days, killing tens of thousands. The city was rebuilt with buildings designed to withstand another earthquake, and philosophers such as Voltaire and Rousseau argued over why such disasters happen.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Lisbon earthquake of 1755

source2.name: Cambridge University Library, Languages across Borders blog, Sonia Morcillo, 'The Lisbon earthquake of 1755'

title: A King Orders Potatoes Planted
text: Many Europeans distrusted the potato, a newcomer from the Andes. In 1756 Frederick the Great of Prussia issued an order commanding that it be grown as food, though at first his people ignored his decrees. It became a staple, and today visitors still leave potatoes on his grave at his palace of Sanssouci.

source.name: Associated Press (via WDIV ClickOnDetroit): Generations of Germans believe Frederick the Great brought potatoes to Germany. It's a myth

title: A Betrayal at Plassey
text: Robert Clive's East India Company troops faced the far larger army of Bengal's ruler, Siraj ud-Daulah. Clive had secretly promised the throne to Siraj's commander Mir Jafar, whose troops held back. A rainstorm also soaked Siraj's gunpowder. The win gave a trading company control of rich Bengal and began British rule in India.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Battle of Plassey

title: Dream of the Red Chamber
text: Cao Xueqin, a writer from a once-rich family that had fallen on hard times, wrote a huge novel about the rise and fall of a grand household. Copies circulated by hand before being printed in 1791. With hundreds of characters, it is one of China's greatest novels, and its fans even have a name for its study: 'Redology'.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Dream of the Red Chamber / Cao Zhan

title: The Fall of Ayutthaya
text: After a siege of more than a year, a Burmese army captured and burned Ayutthaya, the glittering Siamese capital for over 400 years. Within months a general named Taksin rallied the Siamese, drove out the Burmese and founded a new capital at Thonburi, on the riverbank that is now part of Bangkok.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Historic City of Ayutthaya

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Taksin

title: The Great Bengal Famine
text: After a drought in 1769 and floods in 1770 ruined crops, a terrible famine swept Bengal, now under East India Company control. Millions of people died, possibly a third of the population. The Company kept pressing for high land taxes during the crisis, and its revenue collections in 1771 were even higher.

source.name: Banglapedia (Asiatic Society of Bangladesh): Famine

title: Tea in Boston Harbor
text: Angry about a British tax on tea, colonists, some disguised as Mohawk people, boarded three ships and dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into Boston Harbor. Britain responded with harsh punishments, pushing the thirteen colonies closer to revolution.

source.name: Massachusetts Historical Society: Coming of the American Revolution, Boston Tea Party

title: The 'Friendly Islands' of Tonga
text: James Cook visited Tonga, a Polynesian kingdom with powerful chiefs, in 1773, 1774 and 1777. He nicknamed it the Friendly Islands for the courtesy shown to strangers, and chiefs staged night dances with music for his crews. Yet William Mariner, an Englishman who later lived there, heard that some chiefs had plotted to kill Cook but couldn't agree on a plan.

source.name: Captain Cook Society: A Cook's Tour of Tonga

title: A New Planet from a Back Garden
text: William Herschel, a musician who built his own telescopes, spotted a fuzzy object from his home in Bath. It turned out to be Uranus, the first planet discovered since ancient times. His sister Caroline, who helped him, became a famous astronomer too, finding several comets.

source.name: Herschel Museum of Astronomy (Bath Preservation Trust): FAQs

source2.name: European Space Agency: Caroline and William Herschel, Revealing the invisible

title: The First Hot-Air Balloon Show
text: Paper-maker brothers Joseph and Étienne Montgolfier filled a big cloth-and-paper balloon with hot air from a fire and launched it before a crowd in their hometown. A few months later, a sheep, a duck and a rooster rode one at Versailles. By November, two men flew over Paris.

source.name: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum: Montgolfier Brothers

title: Madagascar's Rice-Field King
text: Ambohimanga, a hilltop royal town, was the cradle of the Merina dynasty. Its king Andrianampoinimerina, who reigned from 1787, reunited the Merina kingdom, which had been split among four warring rulers, and gave it uniform laws. He reportedly told his son that the sea should be the edge of his rice fields, meaning the kingdom should cover the whole island.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Madagascar, Political evolution from 1650 to 1810 (Aidan Southall)

title: A Lunar New Year Victory
text: Nguyễn Huệ, a leader of the Tây Sơn rebels, crowned himself Emperor Quang Trung and rushed his army north. During the Tết New Year holiday, his troops surprised and routed a large Qing army occupying Thăng Long, today's Hanoi. The victory is still celebrated at the Đống Đa festival each year.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Tay Son Brothers / history of Vietnam

title: Kamehameha Wins Oʻahu
text: Kamehameha invaded Oʻahu with about 10,000 soldiers and drove its defenders up Nuʻuanu Valley. Hundreds of them, and some of their families, jumped or were forced to their deaths from the steep cliffs at the valley's head rather than accept defeat. The victory made Kamehameha ruler of most of the Hawaiian Islands, and Kauaʻi joined his kingdom peacefully in 1810.

source.name: Library of Congress Subject Headings: Nuʻuanu, Battle of, Oahu, Hawaii, 1795

title: King Jeongjo's Fortress of Filial Love
text: King Jeongjo built Hwaseong Fortress near the tomb of his father, who had died tragically. Scholar Jeong Yak-yong designed cranes and pulleys that sped up construction. The builders kept such detailed records that the walls could be faithfully restored after damage in the Korean War.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Hwaseong Fortress

title: A Milkmaid's Secret Beats Smallpox
text: Country doctor Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who caught mild cowpox seemed safe from deadly smallpox. He took material from a milkmaid's cowpox sore and scratched it into the arm of a boy, James Phipps, who then resisted smallpox. The word 'vaccine' comes from vacca, Latin for cow.

source.name: Riedel S., 'Edward Jenner and the history of smallpox and vaccination', Proc (Bayl Univ Med Cent) 2005, PubMed Central
